cards.question: In one phrase, what is a thread?
cards.answer: An independent execution context (stream of instructions) within a single process.
distractors: A separate program with its own address space.
A copy of a process created by fork().
A kernel data structure that maps pages.

cards.question: In the toy-shop analogy, what does a "thread" correspond to?
cards.answer: A worker in the toy shop (active, works simultaneously with others, needs coordination).
distractors: An order of toys.
The toy shop manager.
A toy part in storage.

cards.question: Why must a process have multiple threads to use multiple CPUs/cores?
cards.answer: A single execution context (one PC/stack/registers) can only run on one CPU at a time.
distractors: The OS limits each process to one CPU unless it forks.
One thread can run on many CPUs, but only slowly.
Multiple threads are needed only for I/O, not for CPUs.

cards.question: What do threads in the same process share?
cards.answer: The entire virtual address space (code, data, file mappings).
distractors: Their stacks and registers.
Only the code segment; data is private.
Nothing; each thread has its own address space.

cards.question: What per-thread state must each thread keep separate, even though it shares an address space?
cards.answer: Its own program counter, stack pointer, stack, and registers.
distractors: Its own page table and heap.
Its own code segment and open files.
Its own virtual address space.

cards.question: How does a multithreaded process's PCB differ from a single-threaded one?
cards.answer: One shared section (address space, code/data) plus separate per-thread execution-context info for each thread.
distractors: Each thread gets a complete copy of the PCB.
It's identical; the OS doesn't track threads.
It stores only the threads' stacks, not the address space.

cards.question: Do threads or processes usually result in hotter caches when several execute concurrently?
cards.answer: Threads — since they share an address space, one thread's cached data is often useful to another.
distractors: Processes — each has its own cache region.
Neither; they're always identical.
Processes — they never share data, so no cache conflicts.

cards.question: Why do threads context-switch faster than processes?
cards.answer: They share the same virtual-to-physical mappings, so no new address-space mapping has to be created.
distractors: They don't save any registers when switching.
They skip the scheduler entirely.
They run in kernel mode, where switches are free.

cards.question: Do both processes and threads have their own execution context (stack + registers)?
cards.answer: Yes — both do.
distractors: Only processes do.
Only threads do.
Neither; the CPU tracks it instead.

cards.question: Do both processes and threads use some communication mechanism between execution contexts?
cards.answer: Yes — processes use IPC; threads synchronize via shared memory.
distractors: No — threads never need to coordinate.
Only processes do; threads use IPC too.
No — both rely only on the scheduler.

cards.question: Give 2 reasons multithreading is more resource-efficient than an equivalent multi-process design.
cards.answer: Threads share one address space (no duplicate memory allocation) and communicate via shared memory instead of costlier IPC.
distractors: Threads get their own address space and use IPC for everything.
Threads skip context switches entirely and use less CPU.
Threads don't need stacks and don't need synchronization.

cards.question: How does splitting work across specialized threads (vs. generic ones) improve performance?
cards.answer: Each thread repeatedly touches a smaller code/data footprint, so it runs with a hotter cache.
distractors: Each thread gets its own dedicated CPU core.
Specialized threads avoid context switches entirely.
Specialized threads need no synchronization.

cards.question: Why is multithreading useful even on a single CPU?
cards.answer: It lets the CPU switch to another thread during one thread's I/O wait, hiding idle time.
distractors: It's not — threads only help with multiple CPUs.
It doubles the CPU's clock speed.
It removes the need for the scheduler.

cards.question: Under what condition does it make sense to switch to another thread instead of just waiting on I/O?
cards.answer: When the expected idle time exceeds roughly 2x the context-switch cost.
distractors: When idle time is less than the context-switch cost.
Always — switching is free.
Only when the idle time exceeds 100× the switch cost.

cards.question: Why is hiding I/O latency cheaper with threads than with processes?
cards.answer: Thread context switches skip recreating virtual-to-physical address mappings, so they're faster.
distractors: Threads don't need to save any registers.
Threads never block on I/O.
Threads run with interrupts disabled.

distractors: It makes each system call faster.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread model, what does the thread data structure store?

distractors: The page table and the list of open files.
The address space and the heap.

cards.question: What does join() do in Birrell's thread model?

cards.question: Why do concurrently running threads risk data races even though processes don't (by default)?

distractors: Threads run in kernel mode.

cards.question: What is mutual exclusion?

distractors: Letting all threads run the same code at once.
Giving each thread its own address space.

cards.question: What is a mutex?
cards.answer: A lock construct that gives one thread at a time exclusive access to a shared resource.
distractors: A queue where threads wait for a condition.

cards.question: What is a deadlock?

distractors: Both threads lock A first, then B.

distractors: Any thread holding more than one lock.
A thread waiting longer than its timeslice.

cards.question: Describe the One-to-One threading model.

distractors: One blocking thread blocks the whole process.

cards.question: What's the main downside of the Many-to-Many model?

cards.question: If a thread signals one condition variable before another, will the first one's waiters run first?
cards.answer: No. The scheduler decides who runs first.
cards.memory: Code order ≠ run order.
distractors: Yes. The first signaled CV always runs first.
Yes. Broadcast always beats signal.
Only on single-CPU systems.

cards.question: Two threads lock mutexes A and B in opposite orders and deadlock. Why doesn't fine-grained locking (unlock A, then lock B) fix it?
cards.answer: The code needs A and B held together.
cards.memory: Fine-grained only works if you need one lock at a time.
distractors: Fine-grained locking always deadlocks more.
Unlocking A isn't allowed while holding B.
It works; it's the standard fix.

cards.question: Two threads lock mutexes A and B in opposite orders and deadlock. What does replacing A and B with one big lock cost?
cards.answer: Parallelism: only one thread at a time.
cards.memory: One giant lock = one thread at a time.
distractors: Memory: each lock needs its own stack.
Correctness: it can deadlock.
Nothing; it's the standard solution.

cards.question: Deadlock handling beyond lock ordering (checking every lock request for cycles, or detecting deadlocks and rolling back): what do these techniques have in common?
cards.answer: They're expensive; used mostly in performance-critical systems.
cards.memory: Prevention and detection cost a lot; lock order is the cheap fix.
distractors: They're free and used everywhere.
They require only one mutex.
They need special hardware.

cards.question: Lecture toy-shop boss-workers example (each order has 6 steps): which step does the boss do?
cards.answer: Only step 1 (accept the order).
cards.memory: The boss hands off immediately to stay fast.
distractors: Steps 1–6 (everything).
Only step 6 (ship the order).
Steps 1 and 2 (accept and parse).

cards.question: In the boss-workers pattern, what is the advantage of the boss handing work directly to a free worker (a handshake)?
cards.answer: Workers don't need to synchronize with each other.
cards.memory: Each worker gets its own direct order: no tray fights.
distractors: The boss does less work per order.
Throughput goes up.
Workers can share one queue.

cards.question: In the boss-workers pattern, what is the drawback of the boss handing work directly to a free worker (a handshake)?
cards.answer: The boss tracks and waits on workers, so throughput drops.
cards.memory: The boss becomes a babysitter.
distractors: Workers must synchronize on a shared queue.
The boss needs a thread pool.
Workers lose locality.

cards.question: In the boss-workers pattern, what happens when the shared work queue is full?
cards.answer: The boss waits, so throughput drops.
cards.memory: Full tray → the boss stands and waits.
distractors: Workers stop processing.
Orders are dropped silently.
The boss creates one new worker per order.

cards.question: In the boss-workers pattern with a dynamic thread pool, how does the pool grow when work piles up?
cards.answer: Several threads at a time, not one per request.
cards.memory: Hire in batches.
distractors: One thread per incoming request.
It never grows; the size is fixed.
It doubles on every request.

cards.question: What is the benefit of the layered pattern over a pipeline?
cards.answer: Coarser, so choosing threads per layer is easier.
cards.memory: Fewer, bigger groups = fewer sizing decisions.
distractors: Work only moves forward.
It needs no synchronization.
Each layer uses a single thread.

cards.question: Boss-workers with specialized workers: besides better cache locality, what else do specialized workers let you do?
cards.answer: Give important tasks or customers higher priority.
cards.memory: VIP customers get more workers.
distractors: Remove the need for a boss.
Avoid all synchronization.
Share one stack across threads.

cards.question: Besides running user-level threads, what else do kernel-level threads run?
cards.answer: OS services such as daemons and drivers.
cards.memory: The kernel has its own staff too.
distractors: User applications' main() functions.
The page tables.
Only interrupt handlers.
